title: Oil above 105 dollars, a hawkish Fed and an RBI cash drain hand Dalal Street a fifth straight weekly loss
standfirst: Crude oil surging on West Asia supply fears was the story of the week, dragging the Nifty and Sensex to a fifth consecutive weekly fall, pushing the rupee to about 95.5 per dollar and lifting India's 10-year bond yield above 7 percent. The RBI spent the week draining surplus liquidity and selling dollars, while hot US inflation flipped expectations from a Fed rate cut to a near-certain hike and the ECB raised rates to 2.5 percent. The week ended with the RBI forcing Tata Sons toward a listing and BRICS leaders gathering in New Delhi.

items.text: The Nifty fell 2.1 percent to 23,398.10 and the Sensex 2.3 percent to 74,781.76, a fifth straight weekly loss, as crude oil, rising US yields and the RBI's liquidity drain weighed on sentiment. Metal stocks fell up to 5 percent and HDFC Bank hit a 52-week low.
The rupee logged its sharpest weekly fall in four months, sliding past 95.5 to end at 95.54, even as the RBI sold dollars and used FX swaps to slow the decline.

The RBI drained surplus banking cash through a 26-day VRRR auction and OMO bond sales, and India's 10-year yield crossed 7 percent after a trimmed debt auction. Governor Malhotra said nothing is off the table, while August retail inflation is estimated at a 20-month high near 4.9 percent, narrowing room for an October rate cut.

SEBI's month-old closing auction session produced 1,000-point Sensex swings on expiry day, prompting a weekend consultation paper with two options for expiry-day settlement. SEBI and the RBI also launched a Demat 2.0 pilot, and MSE settled India's first tokenised corporate bond.

The RBI rejected Tata Sons' bid to stay an unlisted NBFC, forcing the Rs 2.01 lakh crore holding company toward an IPO within three years, while HDFC Bank sent two names to the RBI for its next CEO and Adani Ports settled disclosure proceedings with SEBI.

Brent crude surged past 105 dollars and neared 110 midweek on unresolved West Asia tensions, ending the week up 9.5 percent at 104.61 dollars. On Saturday Saudi Arabia shut the East-West pipeline it uses to bypass the Strait of Hormuz after drone attacks.

US consumer inflation rose 3.4 percent year on year in August with hot producer prices earlier in the week, pushing the odds of a Fed hike at the September 16-17 meeting to about 90 percent. The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.97 percent, its highest since 2023.
The ECB raised rates to 2.5 percent and signalled more hikes may follow if energy prices stay high, with policymaker Kaasik saying market pricing for further tightening is understandable.
Wall Street ended the week lower despite a Friday rebound, with the S&P 500 down 1.2 percent and the Dow down 2.1 percent, while Japan's Nikkei lost 1.6 percent and Hong Kong's Hang Seng 3.3 percent.

India hosted the BRICS summit, where leaders adopted a consensus declaration opposing carbon border taxes and unilateral tariffs, and Modi held talks with Putin and Xi. The US-Canada trade war deepened and Washington finalised duties on Indian solar panels.
